passages.title: The Trans-Saharan Trade Network: A Forgotten Catalyst of Civilisation
passages.content:
[A] For centuries, the vast expanse of the Sahara Desert, stretching over 9 million square kilometres, was perceived by external civilisations as an impassable barrier, isolating the diverse cultures of North Africa from those further south. However, this perception vastly underestimates the ingenuity and resilience of ancient peoples. Far from being an impediment, the Sahara became a crucial artery, facilitating one of the most significant and enduring trade networks in human history: the Trans-Saharan Trade. This intricate system of routes, which flourished for over 1,500 years, connected sub-Saharan Africa with North Africa, Europe, and the Middle East, profoundly shaping the economic, political, and cultural landscapes of the regions it traversed. Its impact was so monumental that entire empires rose and fell based on their control of its vital corridors and lucrative commodities.

[B] The origins of the Trans-Saharan Trade can be traced back to prehistoric times, with evidence of localised exchange across the desert dating as far back as 3000 BCE. Early trade relied on donkey caravans and human porters, limiting the scope and volume of goods. A transformative development arrived with the introduction of the camel from Arabia around the 1st century CE. Camels, perfectly adapted to arid environments, could travel long distances without water, carry heavy loads, and endure harsh desert conditions, revolutionising desert transport. This 'ship of the desert' enabled merchants to traverse the Sahara more efficiently and safely, opening up hitherto inaccessible markets and significantly increasing the scale of trade. By the 8th century, with the expansion of Islamic empires across North Africa, the trade routes became increasingly sophisticated and vital, fueled by growing demand for exotic goods in the burgeoning markets of the Islamic world and beyond.

[C] The primary commodities driving this immense network were gold from the West African savannah regions (particularly from Ghana, Mali, and Songhai empires) and salt from the desert mines (such as Taghaza and Teghazza). Salt was an essential preservative and dietary necessity for populations south of the Sahara, where it was scarce. Gold, on the other hand, was highly coveted in North Africa and Europe, where it formed the backbone of currency systems. Other valuable goods included slaves, ivory, kola nuts, textiles, and manufactured goods from North Africa and Europe. Caravans, often comprising thousands of camels and hundreds of merchants, would embark on perilous journeys lasting months, navigating by stars and traditional knowledge of water sources. The organisation of these expeditions was complex, requiring significant capital investment and meticulous planning, often overseen by powerful merchant guilds.

[D] The wealth generated by the Trans-Saharan Trade had a profound impact on the political development of West Africa. Powerful empires like the Kingdom of Ghana (c. 300-1100 CE), the Mali Empire (c. 1235-1600 CE), and the Songhai Empire (c. 1464-1591 CE) rose to prominence largely due to their strategic control over gold production areas and their ability to levy taxes on passing caravans. These empires became centres of learning, art, and religion, attracting scholars and artisans from across the Islamic world. The city of Timbuktu, for instance, in the Mali and later Songhai empires, became a legendary intellectual and spiritual hub, housing vast libraries and universities, whose influence extended across Africa and into the Middle East. Its prosperity was directly linked to its position at the crossroads of major trade routes.

[E] Beyond economics and politics, the Trans-Saharan Trade served as a powerful conduit for cultural and religious diffusion. The most significant cultural impact was the spread of Islam. Arab traders and scholars who traversed the Sahara brought with them not only goods but also their faith, language (Arabic), legal systems, and architectural styles. Many West African rulers and elites converted to Islam, fostering closer ties with North Africa and the broader Islamic world. This led to the establishment of mosques, Islamic schools, and the adoption of Arabic script for administrative purposes. The interaction also facilitated the exchange of scientific knowledge, medical practices, and philosophical ideas, enriching both sides of the Sahara. This fusion of indigenous African traditions with Islamic influences created a unique cultural synthesis evident in many West African societies today.

[F] The decline of the Trans-Saharan Trade began in the 15th and 16th centuries with the advent of European maritime exploration. Portuguese navigators pioneered sea routes along the West African coast, effectively bypassing the Sahara. The establishment of coastal trading posts offered a cheaper, faster, and less perilous alternative for transporting goods, particularly gold and slaves, to Europe. This shift in trade routes drastically reduced the economic importance of the desert corridors. While some Trans-Saharan trade continued on a smaller scale into the 19th century, particularly for local goods, its grand era as the primary conduit for international commerce between sub-Saharan Africa and the wider world was over. The once-bustling desert cities, dependent on caravan traffic, gradually diminished in influence, marking the end of an extraordinary chapter in global history.

[G] Despite its eventual decline, the legacy of the Trans-Saharan Trade remains indelible. It interconnected diverse cultures, fostered the rise of powerful states, and facilitated the spread of knowledge and religion across a vast continent. Modern archaeological findings continue to unearth evidence of its extensive reach and sophisticated organisation, challenging earlier Eurocentric historical narratives that often overlooked the significant contributions of African civilisations. The trade routes, though now mostly dormant, represent an incredible feat of human endeavour, demonstrating how perceived natural barriers can, with innovation and determination, be transformed into channels of prosperity and cultural exchange. Understanding this network offers crucial insights into the complexities of pre-colonial African societies and their profound interconnectedness with the global arena.

passages.title: Mycorrhizal Networks: The 'Wood Wide Web' of Fungi and Plants
passages.content:
[A] For centuries, the intricate world beneath our feet remained largely unseen and misunderstood, particularly the complex relationships between plants and fungi. While fungi were often considered decomposers or pathogens, their symbiotic role in supporting plant life was only truly appreciated in the late 19th century with the pioneering work of German botanist A.B. Frank. He coined the term "mycorrhiza" in 1885, combining the Greek words for "fungus" (mykes) and "root" (rhiza), to describe the mutualistic association between plant roots and fungal hyphae. This partnership, now known to be ubiquitous across most terrestrial ecosystems, forms the bedrock of soil health and nutrient cycling, enabling plants to thrive in conditions where they would otherwise struggle.

[B] Mycorrhizal associations are broadly categorised into two main types: ectomycorrhizae and endomycorrhizae (which include arbuscular mycorrhizae, or AM). Ectomycorrhizae primarily associate with trees and woody plants in temperate and boreal forests, forming a thick sheath, known as a mantle, around the root tip. From this mantle, fungal hyphae extend into the soil, creating a vast network, and also penetrate between the plant's outer root cells, forming a Hartig net. Endomycorrhizae, particularly arbuscular mycorrhizae, are far more widespread, associating with approximately 80% of all land plant species, including most crops. AM fungi penetrate *into* the plant root cells, forming highly branched structures called arbuscules, where nutrient exchange occurs, and also storage vesicles. Unlike ectomycorrhizae, AM fungi do not form a visible mantle on the root surface.

[C] The core benefit of the mycorrhizal partnership lies in nutrient acquisition. Plants, through photosynthesis, produce sugars (carbohydrates). Fungi, lacking chlorophyll, cannot photosynthesise and thus obtain these essential carbon compounds directly from the plant. In return, the fungal mycelial network, with its exceptionally fine hyphae, extends far beyond the reach of the plant's own root system, vastly increasing the effective surface area for nutrient absorption. Fungi are particularly adept at scavenging for immobile nutrients like phosphorus and certain micronutrients, which are often scarce in soil. They can also access organic forms of nitrogen that are unavailable to plants directly, and some fungal species are known to improve water uptake, enhancing drought resistance for their plant hosts.

[D] Beyond direct nutrient exchange, mycorrhizal networks facilitate interplant communication and resource sharing, earning them the moniker "the Wood Wide Web." Research over the past few decades, spearheaded by scientists like Dr. Suzanne Simard, has revealed that individual plants, even those of different species, can be interconnected via shared fungal networks. This allows for the transfer of carbon, nitrogen, and water from 'donor' plants to 'receiver' plants. For instance, mature "mother trees" in a forest can transfer sugars to shaded seedlings, increasing their survival rates. This resource reallocation is particularly important in stressful environments or during early growth stages. Furthermore, these networks can serve as conduits for warning signals, enabling plants to communicate about pathogen attacks or insect infestations, potentially triggering defence mechanisms in interconnected neighbours.

[E] The ecological implications of these networks are profound. Mycorrhizal fungi play a critical role in soil structure and stability by binding soil particles together with their hyphae and producing glomalin, a sticky glycoprotein. This improves soil aggregation, aeration, and water infiltration, reducing erosion. They are also integral to the decomposition of organic matter and nutrient cycling, contributing significantly to overall ecosystem productivity and biodiversity. Disturbances such as deforestation, excessive tillage, and the application of synthetic fertilisers and fungicides can severely disrupt these delicate networks, leading to reduced plant vigour, increased susceptibility to disease, and degradation of soil quality. Conservation efforts increasingly recognise the importance of protecting and restoring these subterranean partnerships.

[F] The application of mycorrhizal science in agriculture and reforestation is gaining momentum. Farmers are exploring the use of mycorrhizal inoculants to improve crop yields, reduce the need for synthetic fertilisers, and enhance plant resilience against environmental stresses. In forestry, inoculating seedlings with specific mycorrhizal fungi has proven effective in accelerating growth and improving survival rates in challenging planting sites. However, the successful application requires a nuanced understanding of specific plant-fungus interactions, as not all fungal species are compatible with all plant hosts, and environmental conditions can significantly influence the efficacy of the inoculation. Further research is ongoing to harness the full potential of these natural allies in sustainable land management practices.

[G] Despite significant advancements, many aspects of mycorrhizal networks remain a mystery. The sheer diversity of fungal species, the complex genetic interactions, and the dynamic nature of these subterranean communities present ongoing research challenges. New technologies, such as advanced genetic sequencing and imaging techniques, are providing unprecedented insights into the structure and function of these networks. Scientists are also investigating the role of mycorrhizae in carbon sequestration, their response to climate change, and their potential in phytoremediation – the use of plants to clean up contaminated soils. As humanity strives for more sustainable ways to manage natural resources and combat environmental degradation, unlocking the secrets of the mycorrhizal 'Wood Wide Web' will undoubtedly be paramount.

passages.title: The Dawn of Quantum Computing: Principles, Challenges, and Future Prospects
passages.content:
[A] For decades, the computational power of classical computers has advanced at an exponential rate, famously encapsulated by Moore's Law. However, as transistors shrink to atomic scales, the fundamental laws of physics begin to shift from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics, posing inherent limitations to further miniaturisation and processing speed. This looming physical barrier has spurred intensive research into a revolutionary paradigm: quantum computing. Unlike classical bits that represent information as either a 0 or a 1, quantum computers utilise 'qubits,' which can exist in a superposition of both states simultaneously, along with other quantum phenomena like entanglement, to perform calculations in entirely new ways. This offers the potential to tackle problems that are utterly intractable for even the most powerful supercomputers today.

[B] At the heart of quantum computing are two core principles: superposition and entanglement. Superposition allows a qubit to represent a combination of all possible states at once, rather than being confined to a single state. Imagine a spinning coin that is both heads and tails until it lands; a qubit is like that coin in mid-air. This means that a system of 'n' qubits can represent 2^n states simultaneously. Entanglement is an even stranger quantum phenomenon where two or more qubits become intrinsically linked, regardless of the physical distance separating them. The state of one entangled qubit instantaneously influences the state of another, even if they are light-years apart. This interconnectedness allows for complex computations and the potential for quantum communication, forming the basis for the exponential speed-up promised by quantum computers.

[C] The process of quantum computation involves several steps. First, qubits are initialised into a known state. Then, quantum gates – the quantum analogue of classical logic gates – are applied to manipulate the qubits' states, exploiting superposition and entanglement to perform computations. Unlike classical gates that produce a definite output, quantum gates operate on the probabilities of qubit states. Finally, the qubits are measured. This measurement collapses the superposition, yielding a classical 0 or 1. Because the results are probabilistic, a quantum computation often needs to be run multiple times to ascertain the most likely correct answer, making error correction a crucial challenge.

[D] Building a functional quantum computer is an immense engineering challenge. Qubits are incredibly fragile and susceptible to "decoherence," where their quantum states collapse due to interaction with their environment (heat, stray electromagnetic fields, vibrations). Maintaining qubits in their quantum state requires extreme isolation, often involving temperatures close to absolute zero (-273.15 °C) or sophisticated electromagnetic shielding. Various physical implementations of qubits are being explored, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. These include superconducting circuits (used by IBM and Google), trapped ions (IonQ), topological qubits, silicon spin qubits, and photonic qubits. Each approach faces hurdles in scalability, error rates, and the ability to maintain quantum coherence for long enough to perform meaningful computations.

[E] Despite these formidable challenges, significant progress has been made. In 2019, Google announced "quantum supremacy," claiming their Sycamore processor performed a specific computational task in 200 seconds that would take the fastest classical supercomputer 10,000 years to complete. While the task was highly specialised and not immediately practical, it demonstrated the potential for quantum computers to outperform classical ones on certain problems. Other companies and research institutions globally are also making rapid strides, with increasing qubit counts and improving coherence times. The field is still in its early "noisy intermediate-scale quantum" (NISQ) era, meaning current machines have limited qubits and are prone to errors, but they are already powerful enough for preliminary research and algorithm development.

[F] The potential applications of quantum computing are vast and transformative, spanning numerous industries. In medicine and materials science, quantum computers could simulate molecular structures with unprecedented accuracy, accelerating drug discovery and the creation of novel materials with bespoke properties. For example, designing a new catalyst for carbon capture or a superconductor at room temperature could be within reach. In finance, they could optimise complex portfolios, detect fraud more effectively, and improve trading strategies. In cryptography, quantum computers pose a threat to current encryption standards, necessitating the development of "quantum-safe" algorithms, but also offer the potential for unhackable quantum communication. They could also revolutionise artificial intelligence, machine learning, and logistics optimisation.

[G] While the full realisation of a universal, fault-tolerant quantum computer is still likely decades away, the current era of NISQ devices is already fostering innovation. Researchers are developing quantum algorithms tailored for specific problems that are achievable even with noisy qubits. Governments and private companies are investing billions, recognising the strategic importance of this technology. The transition from classical to quantum computing will not be an abrupt replacement but rather a symbiotic relationship, where quantum computers act as powerful accelerators for specific tasks, complementing classical supercomputers. The quantum revolution, though nascent, promises to redefine the boundaries of what is computationally possible, ushering in an era of scientific discovery and technological advancement previously confined to the realm of science fiction.

parts.title: Part 1 - Accommodation Booking for International Students
parts.transcript:
Announcer: Hello and welcome to the IELTS Listening test. There are four parts to the test. You will hear each part once only. For each part of the test, there will be time for you to look at the questions and time for you to check your answers. At the end of the test, you will have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.

Now, turn to Part 1.

Announcer: Part 1. You will hear a conversation between an Accommodation Officer and an international student, Preeya, who is calling to inquire about booking university accommodation. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. [Pause 10]

Accommodation Officer: Good morning, University Accommodation Services, Sarah speaking. How can I help you?

Preeya: Good morning, Sarah. My name is Preeya Singh, S-I-N-G-H. I’m an international student from Thailand, and I’ll be starting my postgraduate studies in September. I’m calling to inquire about booking a room in one of the university's halls of residence.

Accommodation Officer: Ah, welcome, Preeya. Glad to hear you’re considering staying with us. We have several options available for postgraduate students. First, could I get a few more details from you? What’s your student ID number, if you have one already?

Preeya: Yes, I do. It’s 2024-PS-733. That’s two-zero-two-four-P-S-seven-three-three.

Accommodation Officer: Thank you. And your date of birth, please?

Preeya: It’s the 15th of June, 2003.

Accommodation Officer: Okay, 15th June, 2003. Got it. And what course will you be studying, Preeya?

Preeya: I’ll be doing a Master of Science in Environmental Engineering. It's a one-year program.

Accommodation Officer: Environmental Engineering, excellent choice. And could you confirm your current email address for me, please? We'll send all correspondence there.

Preeya: Of course. It’s preeya.singh@email.com. That’s p-r-e-e-y-a.s-i-n-g-h@email.com.

Accommodation Officer: Perfect. Thank you for that. Now, before we move on to the types of accommodation, do you have any specific requirements, perhaps concerning accessibility or medical needs?

Preeya: No, no specific requirements like that, thank you. I’m quite flexible.

Announcer: Now you will hear the rest of the conversation. So, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. [Pause 10]

Accommodation Officer: Right then, Preeya. Our postgraduate accommodation options are primarily in two main halls: Newton Hall and Maxwell House. Newton Hall is our newest building, offering self-catered studio apartments, each with its own kitchenette and bathroom. Maxwell House has individual bedrooms within shared flats, where you’d share a kitchen and living area with three to five other students. It’s also self-catered, of course.

Preeya: Hmm, I’m looking for something that’s not too expensive, but I also value my own space. What are the main differences in terms of cost and facilities?

Accommodation Officer: Well, Newton Hall studios are definitely more private, as you have everything in your own unit. They cost £200 per week. Maxwell House, being shared accommodation, is a bit more economical at £150 per week. Both halls include all utility bills, like electricity, gas, and water, in the rent. Internet access is also free in both.

Preeya: Okay, £150 sounds more within my budget. So, Maxwell House offers shared kitchens. Are they well-equipped?

Accommodation Officer: Absolutely. Each shared kitchen in Maxwell House comes with a fridge-freezer, an oven, a microwave, and a hob. We also provide basic cooking utensils, pots, and pans, though most students prefer to bring their own. There's also a shared laundry room available for residents in Maxwell House, which has washing machines and dryers.

Preeya: That's good to know. And what about social facilities? Are there common areas?

Accommodation Officer: Yes, Newton Hall has a small communal lounge, primarily for quiet study or casual meetings. Maxwell House, on the other hand, has a much larger common room with a television, comfortable seating, and even a games table, making it a more vibrant social hub. It also has a dedicated study room, which many students find very useful.

Preeya: That sounds appealing. I think Maxwell House might be a better fit for me, especially for the social aspect and the study room. It’s good to meet other students.

Accommodation Officer: I agree, it’s a great way to meet people. Just to confirm, are you looking for a single room then, in a shared flat at Maxwell House?

Preeya: Yes, that’s right. A single room. And is it possible to choose who I share with, or is it random?

Accommodation Officer: We do try to match students based on general preferences, for example, quiet students together, or if you have specific requests, we can try to accommodate them, but it’s not guaranteed. You can indicate any preferences on the application form. We typically require a deposit equivalent to four weeks' rent upon booking confirmation.

Preeya: Okay, I understand. So, the deposit for Maxwell House would be £600 then?

Accommodation Officer: That’s correct. We'll send you an email with the application link and further details. Please make sure to submit your application and deposit as soon as possible, as rooms are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis.

Preeya: Thank you so much for all the information, Sarah. You’ve been very helpful.

Accommodation Officer: You’re most welcome, Preeya. We look forward to seeing you in September. Goodbye.

Preeya: Goodbye.

Announcer: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers. [Pause 30]

parts.transcript:
Announcer: This is the IELTS Listening test. Part 2. You will hear a recording. First, you have some time to look at the questions. [Pause 10]

Announcer: Now, turn to Part 2.

Announcer: Part 2. You will hear a tour guide giving an orientation tour of the university campus to new students. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. [Pause 10]

Tour Guide: Good morning, everyone, and a very warm welcome to Westford University! My name is Mark, and I'll be your guide today on this orientation tour of our beautiful campus. We're currently standing right outside the Main Gate, just to your left.

Now, if you look at the map I've handed out, you'll see a small circle indicating our current position, which is the Main Entrance. We'll be walking around the central part of the campus.

Let's start our tour by heading straight through the main path. The very first building we'll encounter on our right, just after entering the gate, is the **Administration Building**. This is where you'll find student records, registration services, and the Vice-Chancellor's office. On your map, this corresponds to point **A**.

Continuing along the main path, past the Administration Building, you’ll see a large open green space on your left. This is the **Central Lawn**, a popular spot for students to relax, study outdoors, or just hang out. Directly opposite the Central Lawn, on the right side of the path, is our magnificent **University Library**. It’s a very modern building with extensive resources, including digital access, quiet study zones, and computer labs. This is marked as point **B** on your map.

As we walk further, you'll pass the Library. Then, you'll see a smaller path branching off to the left, which leads to the student residences. But for now, let's keep going straight. The next building on your left, immediately after the Central Lawn and before the sports facilities, is the **Student Union Building**. This is the heart of student life, housing various clubs, societies, and social events. It’s represented by letter **C**.

After the Student Union, still on the left side, you'll find the **Sports Centre**, with its gymnasium, swimming pool, and sports courts. It's quite large. Following the path past the Sports Centre, just beyond it, you'll see a smaller, older-looking building on the right. This building is the **University Theatre**, where various plays and performances are held throughout the year. On your map, this is point **D**.

Finally, if we were to take the path further around the campus, curving to the right after the theatre, the last major building you would come across before looping back towards the Main Gate is the **Lecture Hall Complex**. It’s a series of large auditoriums for big lectures. This is identified as point **E**.

Announcer: Now you will hear the rest of the tour. So, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. [Pause 10]

Tour Guide: So that gives you a good overview of the main academic and social buildings. Now, let me tell you a bit more about some key services.

First up, the **Cafeteria**. It’s not on the main path we just walked, but it’s actually located in the basement of the Student Union Building, which I mentioned earlier, point C. It offers a wide range of food options, from breakfast to dinner, including vegetarian and vegan choices. Many students find it to be quite affordable compared to off-campus eateries. It’s open from 7 AM to 8 PM on weekdays.

Next, for any health concerns, the **University Health Centre** is a vital resource. It’s located just off campus, about a five-minute walk from the Sports Centre. If you exit the Sports Centre and turn right, walk straight for a couple of minutes, you’ll see it on your left. It provides general medical care, counseling services, and emergency first aid. Appointments are recommended for non-urgent matters.

Many of you will be using our **University Bookshop**. This is found directly opposite the Library, across the main path. Remember the Library was point B? The bookshop is right there, making it very convenient to pick up textbooks and stationery. They also sell university merchandise, which is popular among new students.

Now, about transportation. The **Bus Stop** for public transport is situated right outside the Main Gate, where we started. It’s well-served by several local routes, making it easy to travel to the city center or other parts of town. University shuttle buses also depart from this stop, offering free transport to off-campus student accommodation sites.

Lastly, for banking needs, there’s an **ATM** located on the ground floor of the Administration Building, point A. It's available 24/7. And for more complex banking services, there’s a branch of National Bank just across the street from the Main Gate, but the ATM on campus is usually sufficient for daily cash needs.

I hope this tour has been helpful in familiarizing you with our campus. Remember, there are always staff and student volunteers around to help you find your way in the first few weeks. Enjoy your time here at Westford University!

Announcer: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers. [Pause 30]

parts.title: Part 3 - Student Project Discussion: Renewable Energy
parts.transcript:
Announcer: This is the IELTS Listening test. Part 3. You will hear a recording. First, you have some time to look at the questions. [Pause 10]

Announcer: Now, turn to Part 3.

Announcer: Part 3. You will hear three students, Liam, Chloe, and their tutor, Dr. Evans, discussing their group project on renewable energy. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. [Pause 10]

Dr. Evans: Good morning, Liam, Chloe. Please come in. How are you both getting on with your renewable energy project?

Liam: Good morning, Dr. Evans. We're making steady progress, thank you. We’ve spent the last couple of weeks on initial research and outlining our main points.

Chloe: Yes, we’ve decided to focus on three specific types of renewable energy: solar, wind, and geothermal. We feel these offer a good balance of established and emerging technologies.

Dr. Evans: That’s a sensible approach. What specific aspects of each are you looking into?

Liam: For solar, we're concentrating on photovoltaic cells and their efficiency improvements, particularly in urban environments. We've found some interesting data on rooftop installations.

Chloe: And for wind, we’re looking at offshore wind farms, the challenges of their construction, and their energy output compared to onshore farms. The environmental impact is also a key consideration.

Dr. Evans: Excellent. And geothermal? That’s often overlooked.

Liam: For geothermal, we're exploring its potential in regions not typically known for volcanic activity, focusing on enhanced geothermal systems and their economic viability. It’s quite complex, but fascinating.

Dr. Evans: Indeed. So, what have you found to be the most challenging aspect so far?

Chloe: For me, it’s been the sheer volume of information. There's so much research out there, and sifting through it to find reliable, up-to-date sources has been time-consuming. We're trying to use peer-reviewed journals primarily.

Liam: I'd agree with Chloe about the information overload. But I’d also add the data comparison. Trying to find consistent metrics across different studies, especially for economic viability, has been tricky. For instance, the cost per kilowatt-hour can vary wildly depending on the country or the funding model.

Dr. Evans: Yes, that’s a common difficulty with interdisciplinary projects. You need to be very clear about your parameters. Have you considered including a section on policy and government support? That often plays a significant role in the adoption rates of these technologies.

Chloe: We did think about it, but we decided to keep the scope slightly narrower for now, focusing more on the technological and environmental aspects. We felt that adding policy might make the project too broad for the time we have.

Liam: We're planning to mention it briefly in the conclusion, as a factor that influences implementation, but not as a core research area.

Announcer: Now you will hear the rest of the discussion. So, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. [Pause 10]

Dr. Evans: That sounds reasonable. You have to manage your workload. Now, let’s talk about your presentation. How are you planning to structure it?

Chloe: We're thinking of having an introduction that outlines the global energy crisis and the need for renewables. Then, we'll dedicate a section to each energy source: solar, wind, and geothermal, discussing their technology, pros, and cons.

Liam: And for each of those sections, we’re planning to present some key statistics – for example, the percentage of electricity generated from wind in Denmark, or the efficiency rates of new solar panels. We want to make it data-driven.

Dr. Evans: Good. Data is crucial. Are you using any visual aids?

Chloe: Absolutely. We’re preparing a series of slides with infographics, charts, and relevant images. We also want to include a short video clip, maybe a 30-second animation explaining how an offshore wind turbine works, to make it more engaging.

Dr. Evans: Excellent idea. Visuals are vital for keeping your audience's attention, especially with complex topics. What about the conclusion?

Liam: In the conclusion, we aim to summarize our findings and compare the three energy sources, perhaps highlighting which ones have the most immediate potential for widespread adoption, and discussing the challenges for the future. We also want to briefly touch upon the overall global trends in renewable energy investment.

Chloe: And we're going to reserve five minutes at the end for questions from the audience, as you always recommend.

Dr. Evans: That's very professional. Now, a couple of points of feedback. Liam, when you're discussing the economic viability of geothermal, make sure to differentiate between upfront investment costs and long-term operational savings. It's a common area of confusion.

Liam: Okay, I’ll make a note of that, Dr. Evans. That’s a good distinction to highlight.

Dr. Evans: And Chloe, for the environmental impact of offshore wind farms, perhaps consider briefly touching on their potential benefits for marine ecosystems, such as creating artificial reefs, alongside the more commonly discussed negative impacts. It shows a more nuanced understanding.

Chloe: Oh, that’s an interesting point! I hadn’t thought of that positive aspect. I’ll definitely add that in. Thank you!

Dr. Evans: You’re welcome. Overall, it sounds like you’re both on the right track. Just remember to practice your presentation thoroughly, ensure smooth transitions between your sections, and keep an eye on your time limit. You have 20 minutes for the presentation itself, plus five for questions. Any other concerns?

Liam: Not at the moment, Dr. Evans. This feedback has been really helpful.

Chloe: Yes, thank you for your guidance.

Dr. Evans: My pleasure. I look forward to seeing the final presentation. Keep up the good work!

Announcer: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers. [Pause 30]

parts.title: Part 4 - Lecture on Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
parts.transcript:
Announcer: Now, turn to Part 4.

Announcer: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the applications and implications of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. [Pause 15]

Lecturer: Good morning, everyone. Today, we're going to delve into a truly transformative field: the application of Artificial Intelligence, or AI, in healthcare. AI isn't just a futuristic concept anymore; it's rapidly becoming an integral part of modern medicine, promising to revolutionize how we diagnose, treat, and manage diseases.

Let's begin with a brief historical overview. While the term "Artificial Intelligence" was coined in the 1950s, its integration into healthcare is a much more recent phenomenon. Early AI in medicine involved expert systems that replicated human decision-making using rule-based algorithms. However, the real surge in AI's potential began with advancements in machine learning and deep learning, fueled by vast amounts of data and powerful computational capabilities in the last decade.

So, what are some of the key areas where AI is making a significant impact?

Firstly, **Diagnostics**. AI algorithms can analyze medical images like X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans with remarkable speed and accuracy, often surpassing human capabilities in detecting subtle anomalies. For example, AI can assist radiologists in identifying early signs of cancer or neurological disorders. This not only improves diagnostic accuracy but also reduces the time it takes to get a diagnosis, which is crucial for early intervention.

Secondly, **Drug Discovery and Development**. Traditionally, bringing a new drug to market is an incredibly long and expensive process, often taking over a decade and costing billions of dollars. AI can dramatically accelerate this by predicting how drug compounds will interact with biological targets, identifying potential candidates much faster, and even designing new molecules. This significantly reduces the time and resources required for preclinical trials.

Thirdly, **Personalized Medicine**. Every patient is unique, and what works for one person might not work for another. AI can analyze a patient's genetic makeup, lifestyle, medical history, and even environmental factors to recommend highly personalized treatment plans. This moves us away from a 'one-size-fits-all' approach towards treatments tailored to the individual, maximizing effectiveness and minimizing side effects.

Another crucial area is **Predictive Analytics**. By analyzing large datasets of patient information, AI can identify individuals at high risk of developing certain conditions, such as diabetes or heart disease, even before symptoms appear. This allows for proactive interventions and preventive care, potentially saving countless lives and reducing healthcare costs in the long run.

However, despite these immense benefits, the integration of AI into healthcare also presents several **challenges**.

One major concern is **Data Privacy and Security**. Healthcare data is highly sensitive, and the use of AI systems requires access to vast amounts of this information. Ensuring the secure collection, storage, and processing of patient data while adhering to strict privacy regulations is paramount. Breaches could have severe consequences.

Then there's the issue of **Ethical Considerations**. Who is responsible if an AI system makes a diagnostic error that harms a patient? How do we ensure fairness and prevent bias in AI algorithms, especially if they are trained on datasets that don't represent the full diversity of the population? These are complex questions that require careful deliberation.

Another practical challenge is the **Cost of Implementation**. Developing and integrating sophisticated AI systems into existing healthcare infrastructures is incredibly expensive. This can create disparities, with advanced AI treatments potentially only accessible in wealthier regions or to patients who can afford them, exacerbating existing inequalities in healthcare access.

Finally, there's the **Training and Acceptance** among healthcare professionals. Many medical practitioners need to be trained on how to effectively use and interpret AI tools. There can also be resistance to adopting new technologies, particularly if they are perceived as threatening job security or undermining clinical judgment.

In conclusion, Artificial Intelligence holds incredible promise for transforming healthcare, offering unprecedented capabilities in diagnosis, drug development, and personalized treatment. While significant challenges remain, particularly around ethics, data security, and accessibility, ongoing research and collaborative efforts between AI developers, healthcare providers, and policymakers are paving the way for a future where AI plays a central, beneficial role in improving global health outcomes. The journey is complex, but the potential rewards are truly life-changing.

Announcer: That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers. [Pause 60]

Announcer: That is the end of the IELTS Listening Test. You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.

passages.title: The Evolution of Urban Green Spaces: From Ancient Gardens to Modern Parks
passages.content:
[A] Since the dawn of civilization, humans have sought to integrate natural elements into their constructed environments. The concept of urban green spaces, far from being a modern invention, has a rich and complex history, evolving significantly alongside human societies and their understanding of nature's role in daily life. These spaces, whether grand gardens or humble squares, have consistently served a multitude of purposes, reflecting prevailing cultural values, technological capabilities, and social structures. Their transformation from exclusive private domains to accessible public amenities underscores a profound shift in societal priorities concerning health, recreation, and ecological stewardship within the urban fabric.

[B] The earliest manifestations of urban green spaces can be traced back to ancient civilizations. Examples include the legendary Hanging Gardens of Babylon, though their precise nature remains debated by historians, and the meticulously planned pleasure gardens of Egyptian pharaohs. These were typically enclosed, private sanctuaries designed for aesthetic enjoyment, spiritual contemplation, and the display of power and wealth. Roman villas frequently incorporated elaborate gardens, complete with fountains, statues, and exotic flora, serving as extensions of the living space and reflecting the owner's status. Similarly, in ancient Persia, the 'paradise gardens' ('pairidaeza') were formal, geometric enclosures often featuring water channels and fruit trees, symbolizing an ordered cosmos and offering respite from arid landscapes. In these early periods, the primary beneficiaries were the elite, with little to no access for the general populace.

[C] During the European Middle Ages, green spaces primarily took the form of monastic gardens, vital for cultivating medicinal herbs, vegetables, and for quiet reflection. Castle courtyards sometimes included small decorative gardens. With the Renaissance, a new emphasis on classical ideals and artistic expression led to the creation of magnificent formal gardens in Italy and later France, epitomized by the gardens of Versailles. These were monumental landscape architectural achievements, designed to demonstrate human control over nature and to serve as settings for courtly life and grand spectacles. While publicly impressive, they remained extensions of royal or noble estates, inaccessible for casual public use and serving largely ceremonial functions.

[D] The dramatic societal upheaval of the Industrial Revolution in the 18th and 19th centuries fundamentally altered the urban landscape and the perception of green spaces. Rapid, unplanned urbanization led to overcrowded, unsanitary cities characterized by dense housing, factory smoke, and a severe lack of open space. The once-private gardens of the wealthy were overshadowed by the grim reality of industrial squalor, high disease rates, and widespread social unrest. This period sparked a growing awareness among reformers, philanthropists, and public health advocates of the dire need for accessible green areas to improve the physical and moral well-being of the working classes. The city's 'lungs' were seen as essential for public health and civic order.

[E] This newfound understanding gave rise to the Public Parks Movement, particularly prominent in 19th-century Britain and the United States. One of the most influential figures was Frederick Law Olmsted, co-designer of New York City's Central Park, opened in 1857. Central Park was revolutionary; it was a vast, intentionally designed public landscape, offering democratic access to nature and recreation for all citizens, regardless of social standing. Its success inspired similar projects across the globe. Earlier, Birkenhead Park in England, designed by Joseph Paxton and opened in 1847, also served as a model for creating beautiful, accessible public green spaces, specifically intended to offer a moral and physical escape from the hardships of urban life for working-class populations. These parks symbolized a new civic ideal, a commitment to public welfare, and a belief in the restorative power of nature.

[F] The early 20th century saw the expansion of the green space concept beyond individual parks to more integrated urban planning strategies. Ebenezer Howard's Garden City Movement, originating in Britain around the turn of the century, proposed planned communities that combined the benefits of both town and country, featuring generous green belts, tree-lined streets, and communal gardens. This movement profoundly influenced subsequent urban planning principles globally, advocating for a holistic approach to city design that prioritized open spaces, fresh air, and community well-being. The focus shifted from isolated parks to systematic park systems and the idea of 'green infrastructure' that permeates the entire urban environment.

[G] The mid to late 20th century witnessed a broadening of the role of urban green spaces to include ecological considerations and community empowerment. The rise of environmental awareness movements brought attention to the importance of biodiversity conservation within cities. Community gardens, often on previously derelict plots, emerged as popular initiatives, fostering local food production, social cohesion, and environmental education. The concept of linear parks, like New York's High Line, repurposing disused infrastructure into elevated green walkways, demonstrated innovative approaches to reclaiming urban space. Green belts, initially conceived as a means to control urban sprawl, became recognized for their ecological services, providing habitats and regulating local climate, further integrating nature into urban policy frameworks.

[H] In the 21st century, urban green spaces are being re-imagined as critical components of climate-resilient cities and smart urban ecosystems. They are increasingly designed to perform multiple functions: mitigating urban heat island effects, managing stormwater runoff, supporting urban biodiversity, and even facilitating urban agriculture. The integration of technology allows for 'smart parks' with sensor-driven irrigation and interactive features. Moreover, there is a growing recognition of the profound impact of green spaces on mental health and well-being, leading to designs that prioritize contemplative zones, sensory gardens, and spaces for social interaction. Urban planners now see green spaces not just as amenities, but as essential infrastructure that delivers vital ecosystem services and improves overall quality of life.

[I] From the secluded havens of ancient royalty to the sprawling, multi-functional public parks of today, the evolution of urban green spaces mirrors humanity's changing relationship with nature and its understanding of the city itself. While challenges such as equitable access, funding, and maintenance persist, the ongoing innovation in design and the increasing recognition of their ecological, social, and economic benefits affirm their indispensable role. As urban populations continue to grow, the thoughtful creation and preservation of green spaces will remain paramount for fostering healthy, sustainable, and livable cities for future generations, serving as vital connectors between human civilization and the natural world.

passages.title: The Enigmatic Glow: Bio-luminescence in Deep-Sea Ecosystems and Its Applications
passages.content:
[A] Bio-luminescence, the production of light by living organisms, is one of nature's most captivating phenomena. From the familiar flicker of a firefly on a summer night to the ghostly glow of fungi in a dark forest, light-emitting life forms have fascinated humans for centuries. However, it is in the vast, dark expanse of the deep ocean, where sunlight never penetrates, that bio-luminescence truly reigns supreme. Here, an astonishing 90% of all known deep-sea creatures are thought to be bio-luminescent, utilizing light for survival in ways that continue to amaze scientists and inspire technological innovation. This natural light show is not merely for aesthetic display; it is a critical tool in the struggle for existence in the most extreme environment on Earth.

[B] The production of bio-luminescence is fundamentally a chemical reaction. At its core, it involves a molecule called luciferin, which is the substrate that produces light, and an enzyme, luciferase, which acts as a catalyst to speed up the reaction. In the presence of oxygen and often adenosine triphosphate (ATP) – the energy currency of the cell – luciferin is oxidized, releasing energy in the form of light rather than heat, a process known as 'cold light' emission. The specific chemical structures of luciferin and luciferase vary widely across different species, leading to a diverse palette of colors, from blue and green (most common in marine environments) to yellow and red (more prevalent in terrestrial organisms). This biochemical versatility underscores millions of years of evolutionary adaptation.

[C] The deep-sea environment, typically defined as waters below 200 meters, presents formidable challenges for life. Characterized by perpetual darkness, immense pressure, near-freezing temperatures, and scarcity of food, it is an ecosystem where every survival mechanism must be highly specialized and efficient. In this lightless realm, where visual cues from the sun are entirely absent, bio-luminescence has evolved as a paramount form of communication and interaction. Without it, many deep-sea creatures would be utterly blind and unable to find mates, evade predators, or capture prey, transforming the abyss into an even more inhospitable place.

[D] Deep-sea creatures employ bio-luminescence for a bewildering array of functions. One of the most sophisticated uses is camouflage, particularly 'counter-illumination'. Many species possess photo-phores (light-producing organs) on their undersides that emit light matching the faint down-welling light from the surface (or the bio-luminescence of other creatures). This cleverly masks their silhouette, making them invisible to predators hunting from below. For predation, some species, like the iconic anglerfish, use bio-luminescent lures dangling from a modified dorsal fin to attract unsuspecting prey directly to their mouths. Others use brief, intense flashes to temporarily blind or disorient prey, making capture easier. Defensive strategies include startling predators with sudden bursts of light, creating 'smoke screens' of glowing particles to escape, or even 'burglar alarms' where a creature lights up to attract a larger predator to consume its attacker.

[E] Specific examples illustrate these ingenious tactics. The flashlight fish (Anomalops katoptron) harbors symbiotic bacteria in sub-orbital organs, which they can 'turn off' using a shutter-like mechanism to blink in Morse-code-like patterns for communication or to evade predators. Certain species of squid and octopus can squirt clouds of bio-luminescent fluid, similar to ink, to confuse attackers. Some jellyfish, when disturbed, produce dazzling waves of light that travel around their bell, a 'burglar alarm' to summon larger predators. The tiny copepods and krill, despite their size, can emit bright flashes to deter predators, making them a less appealing target. Even some deep-sea sharks exhibit bio-luminescence, potentially for counter-illumination or to blend into the bio-luminescent background of their prey.

[F] While most pronounced in marine environments, bio-luminescence is also found in terrestrial organisms, albeit with different ecological contexts and chemical mechanisms. The most famous example is the firefly (Lampyridae), which uses its rhythmic flashes for mating signals. Millipedes, earthworms, and various fungi (e.g., foxfire) also produce light, often for defense or to attract spore-dispersing insects. These terrestrial forms typically emit yellow or green light and represent independent evolutionary pathways compared to their marine counterparts, highlighting the convergent evolution of light production across disparate life forms under different selective pressures.

[G] Beyond its ecological marvel, bio-luminescence has become an invaluable tool in scientific research and medical diagnostics. The gene for Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP), originally isolated from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria, has revolutionized cell biology. Scientists can fuse GFP to other proteins, making them glow and allowing researchers to visualize gene expression, protein localization, and cellular processes in living organisms without invasive techniques. Bio-luminescent assays are used in drug discovery, environmental monitoring (e.g., detecting pollutants by observing changes in bacterial luminescence), and in detecting bacterial contamination in food and water. This allows for sensitive, non-toxic, and often real-time insights into biological systems.

[H] The potential future applications of bio-luminescence extend into numerous innovative fields. Researchers are exploring the possibility of developing self-sustaining, bio-luminescent streetlights or indoor lighting systems that are energy-efficient and environmentally friendly, potentially powered by engineered bacteria or plants. In medicine, bio-luminescent reporters could offer enhanced in-vivo imaging for earlier disease detection, particularly in cancer research, and more precise drug delivery monitoring. Imagine bio-luminescent plants acting as natural biosensors for environmental toxins or even glowing trees replacing traditional streetlamps, reducing our carbon footprint.

[I] However, harnessing the full potential of bio-luminescence comes with its own set of challenges and ethical considerations. The complexity of bio-luminescent systems means that successful genetic engineering for practical applications requires a deep understanding of intricate biochemical pathways. There are also concerns about the ecological impact of introducing genetically modified organisms into natural environments, even if for beneficial purposes. The cost and scalability of developing bio-luminescent technologies remain significant hurdles. Furthermore, ethical questions regarding the manipulation of life forms for human benefit must be carefully addressed as research progresses.

[J] In conclusion, bio-luminescence stands as a testament to the extraordinary adaptability of life. From its role as a fundamental survival mechanism in the profound depths of the ocean to its transformative potential in laboratories and future technologies, this enigmatic glow continues to illuminate our understanding of the natural world and inspire innovative solutions for humanity's most pressing challenges. The future promises even more astonishing discoveries and applications as we continue to unlock the secrets held within this living light.

questions.text: What is the primary reason bio-luminescence is so prevalent in the deep ocean?
options: A. Deep-sea creatures need to generate heat due to cold temperatures.
B. Sunlight cannot penetrate the deep ocean, making light production essential for survival.
C. The high pressure in the deep sea enhances the chemical reactions for light production.
D. Bio-luminescence is a byproduct of the abundant food sources in the deep ocean.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph C อธิบายว่าสภาพแวดล้อมใต้ทะเลลึกถูกกำหนดโดย 'perpetual darkness' (ความมืดมิดตลอดกาล) และ 'In this lightless realm... bio-luminescence has evolved as a paramount form of communication and interaction.' (ในอาณาจักรที่ไร้แสงนี้... การเรืองแสงทางชีวภาพได้วิวัฒนาการขึ้นเป็นรูปแบบการสื่อสารและการมีปฏิสัมพันธ์ที่สำคัญยิ่ง).

questions.text: According to the passage, what distinguishes bio-luminescence from other forms of light production?
options: A. It always produces blue or green light.
B. It is generated through a purely physical reaction.
C. It releases energy primarily as light rather than heat.
D. It is exclusively found in marine organisms.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph B ระบุว่า 'luciferin is oxidized, releasing energy in the form of light rather than heat, a process known as 'cold light' emission.' (ลูซิเฟรินจะถูกออกซิไดซ์ ปล่อยพลังงานในรูปของแสงมากกว่าความร้อน ซึ่งเป็นกระบวนการที่เรียกว่าการปล่อย 'แสงเย็น').

questions.text: What is a 'burglar alarm' strategy in bio-luminescence, as described in the passage?

B. Creating a flash of light to temporarily blind attackers.
C. Lighting up to attract a larger predator to consume its attacker.

passages.title: Unveiling Distant Worlds: The Search for Exoplanets and the Quest for Life Beyond Earth
passages.content:
[A] For millennia, humanity has gazed upon the stars and pondered the existence of other worlds. What was once the realm of philosophical speculation and science fiction has, in recent decades, transformed into a vibrant and rapidly advancing field of scientific inquiry: exoplanetology. The discovery of planets orbiting stars beyond our Sun – exoplanets – has fundamentally reshaped our understanding of planetary formation, the prevalence of planetary systems, and the potential for life elsewhere in the cosmos. This quest to unveil distant worlds is not merely an academic exercise; it touches upon profound questions about our place in the universe.

[B] The first confirmed discovery of an exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995, marked a watershed moment. Before this, detecting exoplanets was incredibly challenging because they are small, dim, and hidden by the overwhelming glare of their host stars. Early detection methods primarily relied on the 'radial velocity' or 'Doppler spectroscopy' method. This technique involves observing slight 'wobbles' in a star's movement, caused by the gravitational pull of an orbiting planet. When a planet tugs on its star, it causes the star to move slightly towards and away from Earth, leading to measurable shifts in the star's light spectrum. This method was initially biased towards finding massive planets orbiting very close to their stars – dubbed 'Hot Jupiters' – because their gravitational effect is stronger and easier to detect.

[C] The 'transit method' revolutionized exoplanet detection and is responsible for the vast majority of discoveries to date. This method involves observing a slight, periodic dimming of a star's light as a planet passes directly in front of it from our perspective. The amount of dimming can reveal the planet's size relative to its star, and the regularity of the dimming indicates its orbital period. NASA's Kepler Space Telescope, launched in 2009, was a pioneer in this field, staring at a single patch of sky for years, continuously monitoring the brightness of over 150,000 stars. Kepler confirmed thousands of exoplanets, including many smaller, rocky worlds, dramatically expanding our catalog and demonstrating that planetary systems are common throughout the galaxy.

[D] While radial velocity and transit methods are the most prolific, other ingenious techniques contribute to our exoplanet census. 'Direct imaging' involves taking actual pictures of exoplanets, but this is exceedingly difficult due to the brightness of their host stars and the vast distances involved; it typically only works for very large, young planets far from their stars. 'Gravitational microlensing' occurs when a foreground star passes in front of a more distant star, and the gravity of the foreground star (and any planets orbiting it) bends and magnifies the light from the background star. 'Astrometry' is similar to radial velocity but measures the actual tiny side-to-side shift of a star in the sky due to a planet's gravitational pull, rather than its motion towards or away from us. Each method offers unique advantages and limitations, contributing to a more complete picture of exoplanet diversity.

[E] The ultimate goal of exoplanet research is to find habitable worlds – planets capable of supporting life as we know it. This typically requires a planet to reside within its star's 'habitable zone' or 'Goldilocks Zone,' where conditions allow for liquid water to exist on its surface. Beyond temperature, other factors are crucial: a suitable atmospheric composition (e.g., presence of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen), a stable star (not prone to violent flares), a magnetic field to protect against stellar radiation, and the presence of essential building blocks for life. However, life might exist in forms we don't anticipate, challenging our Earth-centric definitions of habitability.

[F] Several exoplanet systems have captured public imagination due to their potential for habitability. The TRAPPIST-1 system, discovered in 2016 and 2017, hosts seven Earth-sized planets, at least three of which are located within its star's habitable zone. Another exciting discovery is Proxima Centauri b, an exoplanet orbiting our nearest stellar neighbor, Proxima Centauri, also within its habitable zone. While these discoveries are thrilling, the actual conditions on these planets are still largely unknown, and questions about their atmospheres, water content, and potential for volcanic activity remain subjects of intense study. They represent our best current candidates for follow-up observations.

[G] Characterizing the atmospheres of exoplanets is the next frontier. Using 'transit spectroscopy,' scientists can analyze the light from a star that passes through an exoplanet's atmosphere during a transit. As the starlight filters through, certain gases in the planet's atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths of light, leaving detectable 'fingerprints' in the spectrum. This allows researchers to infer the chemical composition of exoplanet atmospheres, searching for gases like water vapor, methane, carbon dioxide, and potentially even biosignatures. However, this is an incredibly challenging task, requiring extremely sensitive instruments and sophisticated data analysis, and is currently only feasible for larger planets or those with thick, extended atmospheres.

[H] The search for 'biosignatures' – evidence of past or present life – is a central aim. Biosignatures are specific chemical compounds or combinations of compounds (like oxygen, methane, ozone, and water vapor) that are produced by biological processes. Detecting them in an exoplanet's atmosphere would be a monumental discovery. However, caution is paramount; these gases can also be produced by geological or photochemical processes. Robust evidence would require detecting multiple biosignatures together, understanding the planet's geological context, and ruling out all non-biological explanations. This necessitates advanced observational capabilities and sophisticated modeling.

[I] Future missions and next-generation telescopes are designed to push these boundaries. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in 2021, is already providing unprecedented views of exoplanet atmospheres, capable of detecting the subtle chemical signatures that previous telescopes could not. Upcoming missions like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will significantly expand our ability to perform microlensing surveys and direct imaging. Ground-based observatories, such as the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) under construction, will provide enormous light-gathering power for high-resolution spectroscopy of nearby exoplanets. These instruments are vital for building a comprehensive census of exoplanets and for the detailed characterization needed to find true Earth analogs.

[J] The philosophical implications of exoplanet discovery are profound. The 'Fermi Paradox' asks why, if the universe is teeming with potentially habitable worlds, we haven't yet detected any signs of extraterrestrial civilizations. The 'Drake Equation' is a probabilistic argument used to estimate the number of active, communicative extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way galaxy. While these are theoretical frameworks, they highlight the immense scale of the search and the potential ramifications of finding life – or finding none at all – for humanity's self-perception and understanding of its unique place (or lack thereof) in the cosmos.

[K] In conclusion, the field of exoplanetology has moved from the realm of science fiction to cutting-edge empirical science in a remarkably short time. Each new discovery refines our models of planetary formation and provides fresh insights into the diversity of worlds. The ultimate goal – detecting life beyond Earth – remains elusive but increasingly plausible. As technology advances and our understanding deepens, the prospect of answering one of humanity's oldest and most profound questions about whether we are alone in the universe draws ever closer.

questions.text: What was the main limitation of the radial velocity method when it was first used?
options: A. It could only detect very small planets far from their stars.
B. It was biased towards finding large planets orbiting close to their stars.
C. It was unable to distinguish between a star's wobble and its natural rotation.
D. It required direct imaging, which was technically impossible.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph B ระบุว่า 'This method was initially biased towards finding massive planets orbiting very close to their stars – dubbed 'Hot Jupiters' – because their gravitational effect is stronger and easier to detect.' (วิธีนี้แต่เดิมมีอคติในการค้นหาดาวเคราะห์ขนาดใหญ่ที่โคจรรอบดาวฤกษ์ของพวกมันอย่างใกล้ชิด – ซึ่งถูกเรียกว่า 'Hot Jupiters' – เพราะผลกระทบจากแรงโน้มถ่วงของพวกมันแข็งแกร่งกว่าและตรวจจับได้ง่ายกว่า).

questions.text: Which exoplanet detection method is described as observing a star's periodic dimming?
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph C อธิบายว่า 'The 'transit method'... involves observing a slight, periodic dimming of a star's light as a planet passes directly in front of it from our perspective.' (วิธี 'การเคลื่อนผ่าน' ... เกี่ยวข้องกับการสังเกตการหรี่แสงเล็กน้อยและเป็นคาบของดาวฤกษ์เมื่อดาวเคราะห์เคลื่อนผ่านหน้าดาวฤกษ์จากมุมมองของเรา).

questions.text: What is the primary characteristic of the 'Goldilocks Zone' in relation to exoplanets?
options: A. It is the region where exoplanets are most likely to be directly imaged.
B. It is the distance from a star where liquid water can exist on a planet's surface.
C. It is the area where the star's gravitational pull is strongest, causing significant wobbles.
D. It refers to a planet's atmospheric composition being similar to Earth's.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph E อธิบายว่า 'This typically requires a planet to reside within its star's 'habitable zone' or 'Goldilocks Zone,' where conditions allow for liquid water to exist on its surface.' (โดยทั่วไปสิ่งนี้ต้องให้ดาวเคราะห์อยู่ใน 'เขตที่อยู่อาศัย' หรือ 'โซน Goldilocks' ของดาวฤกษ์ ซึ่งมีสภาพที่เอื้อให้มีน้ำในสถานะของเหลวอยู่บนพื้นผิวได้).

questions.text: What is the main challenge in using 'direct imaging' for exoplanet detection?
options: A. The exoplanets are too small to be seen.
B. The host star's brightness makes it difficult to see the exoplanet.
C. This method only works for very old planets.
D. It requires planets to have very thick atmospheres.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph D ระบุว่า 'Direct imaging' ... 'is exceedingly difficult due to the brightness of their host stars and the vast distances involved' (ทำได้ยากอย่างยิ่งเนื่องจากความสว่างของดาวฤกษ์แม่และการที่มันอยู่ห่างไกล).

questions.text: Before 1995, scientists had confirmed the existence of many exoplanets.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph B ระบุว่า 'The first confirmed discovery of an exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995, marked a watershed moment.' (การค้นพบดาวเคราะห์นอกระบบสุริยะดวงแรกที่ได้รับการยืนยันว่าโคจรรอบดาวฤกษ์คล้ายดวงอาทิตย์ คือ 51 Pegasi b ในปี 1995 ถือเป็นจุดเปลี่ยนสำคัญ). นั่นหมายความว่าก่อนปี 1995 ยังไม่มีการยืนยันการค้นพบดาวเคราะห์นอกระบบสุริยะ.

questions.text: The Kepler Space Telescope monitored the brightness of over 150,000 stars in a single region of the sky.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph C กล่าวว่า 'NASA's Kepler Space Telescope... staring at a single patch of sky for years, continuously monitoring the brightness of over 150,000 stars.' (กล้องโทรทรรศน์อวกาศเคปเลอร์ของ NASA... จ้องมองพื้นที่เดียวบนท้องฟ้าเป็นเวลาหลายปี โดยตรวจสอบความสว่างของดาวฤกษ์มากกว่า 150,000 ดวงอย่างต่อเนื่อง).

questions.text: The presence of liquid water is the only factor determining a planet's habitability.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph E ระบุว่า 'Beyond temperature, other factors are crucial: a suitable atmospheric composition... a stable star... a magnetic field... and the presence of essential building blocks for life.' (นอกเหนือจากอุณหภูมิแล้ว ปัจจัยอื่นๆ ก็มีความสำคัญ: องค์ประกอบของชั้นบรรยากาศที่เหมาะสม... ดาวฤกษ์ที่เสถียร... สนามแม่เหล็ก... และการมีองค์ประกอบสำคัญสำหรับการดำรงชีวิต). ซึ่งบ่งชี้ว่ามีปัจจัยอื่นๆ นอกเหนือจากน้ำที่เป็นของเหลว.

questions.text: TRAPPIST-1 system contains more Earth-sized planets than Proxima Centauri b's system.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph F ระบุว่า 'The TRAPPIST-1 system... hosts seven Earth-sized planets, at least three of which are located within its star's habitable zone.' (ระบบ TRAPPIST-1... มีดาวเคราะห์ขนาดเท่าโลกเจ็ดดวง โดยอย่างน้อยสามดวงอยู่ในเขตที่อยู่อาศัยของดาวฤกษ์). ในขณะที่ Proxima Centauri b เป็นดาวเคราะห์ดวงเดียวที่กล่าวถึงในระบบนั้น.

questions.text: Transit spectroscopy is currently effective for analyzing the atmospheres of all types of exoplanets.
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph G ระบุว่า 'this is an incredibly challenging task... and is currently only feasible for larger planets or those with thick, extended atmospheres.' (นี่เป็นงานที่ท้าทายอย่างยิ่ง... และปัจจุบันทำได้เฉพาะกับดาวเคราะห์ขนาดใหญ่หรือดาวเคราะห์ที่มีชั้นบรรยากาศหนาและขยายออกไป). ซึ่งหมายความว่าไม่สามารถใช้ได้กับดาวเคราะห์ทุกประเภท.

questions.text: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS: What term is used for the slight changes in a star's light spectrum caused by an orbiting planet?
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph B กล่าวว่า 'leading to measurable shifts in the star's light spectrum.' (นำไปสู่การเปลี่ยนแปลงที่วัดได้ในสเปกตรัมแสงของดาวฤกษ์).

questions.text: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS: Which space telescope was a pioneer in using the transit method for exoplanet detection?
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph C ระบุว่า 'NASA's Kepler Space Telescope, launched in 2009, was a pioneer in this field' (กล้องโทรทรรศน์อวกาศเคปเลอร์ของ NASA ซึ่งเปิดตัวในปี 2009 เป็นผู้บุกเบิกในสาขานี้).

questions.text: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS: What kind of objects does gravitational microlensing typically involve passing in front of a more distant star?
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph D อธิบายว่า 'Gravitational microlensing occurs when a foreground star passes in front of a more distant star' (การหักเหแสงจากแรงโน้มถ่วงขนาดเล็กเกิดขึ้นเมื่อดาวฤกษ์ที่อยู่ด้านหน้าเคลื่อนผ่านหน้าดาวฤกษ์ที่อยู่ไกลออกไป).

questions.text: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS: Which new space telescope is providing unprecedented views of exoplanet atmospheres?
questions.explanation_thai: Paragraph I ระบุว่า 'The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in 2021, is already providing unprecedented views of exoplanet atmospheres' (กล้องโทรทรรศน์อวกาศเจมส์เวบบ์ (JWST) ซึ่งเปิดตัวในปี 2021 กำลังให้มุมมองที่ไม่เคยมีมาก่อนเกี่ยวกับชั้นบรรยากาศของดาวเคราะห์นอกระบบ).

parts.title: Part 1 - Enrolling in a Community Language Course
parts.transcript:
Announcer: Hello and welcome to the IELTS Listening test. There are four parts to the test. You will hear each part once only. For each part of the test, there will be time for you to look at the questions and time for you to check your answers. At the end of the test, you will have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.

Now, turn to Part 1.

Announcer: Part 1. You will hear a conversation between a man, Marco, and a woman at a community centre, who is helping him enrol in a language course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. [Pause 10]

Administrator: Good afternoon, Northwood Community Centre, how can I help you?

Marco: Hello, I'm calling to enrol in one of your language courses.

Administrator: Certainly. Which course are you interested in?

Marco: I'd like to sign up for the evening Spanish course.

Administrator: The Spanish course. Okay, I can help you with that. First, I just need to take a few details. Could I have your full name, please?

Marco: Yes, it’s Marco Ricci. That's Marco, M-A-R-C-O, and my surname is Ricci, R-I-C-C-I.

Administrator: Got it. And a contact phone number?

Marco: My mobile is 07700 900 415.

Administrator: 07700 900 415. Thank you. And what is your occupation?

Marco: I’m a graphic designer.

Administrator: A graphic designer, okay. And could I take an email address for you? We send out confirmations and any class updates by email.

Marco: Of course. It's m.ricci88@emailbox.com.

Administrator: m.ricci, and is that the number eighty-eight?

Marco: Yes, that’s right. at emailbox.com.

Administrator: Perfect. And just for our records, how did you hear about our courses?

Marco: I saw a poster for the centre in my local library.

Announcer: Now you will hear the rest of the conversation. So, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. [Pause 10]

Administrator: Right, Marco. Now, let’s get you enrolled in that Spanish course. We have two evening classes, one on Tuesdays and one on Thursdays. They both run from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. Which would you prefer?

Marco: I work late on Thursdays, so Tuesday would be best for me.

Administrator: Okay, so the Tuesday class. Now, the course is for beginners, is that right?

Marco: Yes, completely. I don't know any Spanish at all.

Administrator: No problem, that’s what it’s for! The course runs for a total of 12 weeks, and the full cost is £180.

Marco: £180, okay. Does that fee include the course textbook?

Administrator: Unfortunately, no. You will need to buy the textbook separately. The book is called '¡Adelante! Uno', and it costs about £25. You can buy it at any good bookshop or online.

Marco: I see. And what about other materials? Will I need a dictionary or anything?

Administrator: A good dictionary is always recommended, but we do provide all other learning materials, you know, handouts, worksheets, and access to our online portal. That’s all included in the course fee.

Marco: And where exactly is the class held?

Administrator: All our evening language classes are in the main building. The Spanish class is in Room 7, which is on the first floor.

Marco: Room 7, okay. And when does the course start?

Administrator: The next course begins on the 21st of September.

Marco: September 21st. Great. So, how do I pay? Can I do it over the phone now?

Administrator: Yes, you can pay by credit or debit card now. I’ll just need your card details…

Announcer: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers. [Pause 30]
